raw_case_text:
This case involves a 33-year-old male artisanal miner with a 14-year work history who presented with an occasional nonproductive cough of 5 years duration. However, the cough became persistent and productive of whitish sputum associated with recurrent breathlessness and low-grade fever over the 2-year period prior to presentation. The patient acknowledged not using personal protective equipment while working. He had no prior comorbidities and initially experienced severe bilateral knee joint pain, which was worse in the mornings. He later developed hypopigmentation and skin thickening on his face, neck, torso, and knees. He visited multiple healthcare facilities on account of the above complaints. At one of such visits, he was prescribed antituberculosis (TB) medication even though the sputum for GeneXpert was negative. His symptoms of exertional dyspnea and cough progressed despite completing a 6-month course of anti-TB medications. This prompted the last attending physician to refer the patient to the Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital.
On examination, he was in respiratory distress with an oxygen saturation of 78% on room air and required oxygen via a nonrebreather mask at 10 L/min, which raised the oxygen saturation to 94%. He was moderately pale, had reduced breath sound intensity (air entry) in the upper and middle lung zones, and had bronchial breath sounds in the right lung zones. Vocal resonance was increased bilaterally in the middle lung zones. He had salt-and-pepper dermopathy with tight and adherent skin on his face, chest, back, and knees (Figures 1(a), 1(b), and 1(c)). He additionally had microstomia, rat bite sign of the fingers, and Raynaud's phenomenon. The Raynaud's phenomenon had been present for close to a year. However, the patient did not have sclerodactyly. He was conscious and alert.
(a-c) Tightened skin with leukoderma, consistent with a "salt-and-pepper" appearance.
Laboratory investigations showed a hemoglobin level of 11.5 g/dL, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 67 mm fall in the first hour, and a C-reactive protein of 41.9 mg/dL. Liver and renal function tests were normal, and negative results were obtained for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C serology. Pulmonary TB was considered as part of the differential diagnosis; however, the sputum for GeneXpert was negative. Antinuclear antibody by indirect immunofluorescence on hep-2 cells was positive (1:320), and Antitopoisomerase 1 antibodies were also positive.
Chest CT scan showed mass-like consolidations with spiculated margins involving both upper lobes and the superior segments of the lower lobes, with parenchymal calcifications seen within the areas of consolidation. There was associated traction bronchiectasis, fibrotic changes, and subpleural cystic changes with mediastinal and left perihilar lymph nodes seen with eggshell-type calcification, findings consistent with complicated silicosis (Figures 2(a) and 2(b)).
(a) Fibrosis of the lung with tram-tract appearance and signet ring appearance of the lung, and reduced lung volume on the left. (b) Presence of radio-opaque silica in both lungs.
Based on his history of exposure, radiological evidence for silicosis, and clinical and laboratory manifestations of SSc, the patient was diagnosed with Erasmus syndrome. He was started on immunosuppressive therapy, including oral prednisolone 60 mg daily, which was tapered to 10 mg daily over 4 weeks, and oral mycophenolate mofetil 1 g 12 hourly. He was also prescribed off-label oral pirfenidone 200 mg 8 hourly and oral omeprazole 20 mg daily. Raynaud's phenomenon was managed with lifestyle modification and tab nifedipine (extended-release) 30 mg daily.
Two weeks postadmission, the patient's oxygen saturation ranged between 88% and 91% on intranasal oxygen at 6 L/min. He was counseled on long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) and discharged home with mobile oxygen. There was no significant improvement 1 month after discharge, with an oxygen saturation of 89% on intranasal oxygen and breathlessness at rest. Unfortunately, the patient passed away 8 weeks postdischarge.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 33-year-old male artisanal miner presented with a 5-year history of cough that became productive of whitish sputum with recurrent breathlessness and low-grade fever over the past 2 years, accompanied by progressive skin tightening and Raynaud's phenomenon.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: After 3 years of occasional dry cough, the patient developed persistent productive cough, exertional and resting dyspnea, and low-grade fever over the 2 years prior to tertiary referral, alongside morning-predominant bilateral knee arthralgias, 1 year of Raynaud's phenomenon, and progressive facial, truncal, and knee skin thickening and depigmentation. At an outside facility, he had completed a 6-month empirical course of anti-TB therapy (despite a negative sputum GeneXpert) with continued respiratory deterioration.
subjective.past_medical_history: 14-year occupational history as an artisanal miner without personal protective equipment; completed 6 months of empirical anti-TB treatment prior to referral.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for productive cough, severe dyspnea, low-grade fever, bilateral knee arthralgia, Raynaud's phenomenon, microstomia, and skin tightening/dyspigmentation; negative for sclerodactyly.

objective.physical_examination: Conscious and alert, in acute respiratory distress with SpO2 78% on room air (improving to 94% on 10 L/min non-rebreather oxygen mask), moderately pale. Chest auscultation revealed reduced air entry in the upper and middle lung zones, right-sided bronchial breath sounds, and bilaterally increased vocal resonance in the middle zones. Cutaneous/rheumatologic exam showed tight, adherent skin with 'salt-and-pepper' leukoderma over the face, neck, chest, back, and knees, microstomia, digital tip 'rat-bite' necrosis/ulcerations, and Raynaud's phenomenon without sclerodactyly.
objective.routine_investigations: Hb 11.5 g/dL, ESR 67 mm/1st hr, CRP 41.9 mg/dL, normal liver and renal function, negative HIV, HBV, and HCV serologies. Sputum GeneXpert MTB/RIF was negative. ANA by indirect immunofluorescence on HEp-2 cells was positive (1:320), and anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) antibodies were positive.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT demonstrated bilateral upper lobe and superior lower-lobe segment mass-like spiculated consolidations containing parenchymal calcifications (progressive massive fibrosis), traction bronchiectasis, subpleural cysts, left lung volume loss, and mediastinal and left perihilar lymph nodes with eggshell calcifications characteristic of complicated silicosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Pulmonary tuberculosis was excluded by repeated negative sputum GeneXpert assays and lack of response to prior 6-month anti-TB therapy, and the patient was diagnosed with Erasmus syndrome (silica-induced systemic sclerosis superimposed on complicated pulmonary silicosis). He was treated with supplemental oxygen, oral prednisolone (60 mg/day tapered to 10 mg/day over 4 weeks), mycophenolate mofetil (1 g BID), off-label pirfenidone (200 mg TID), extended-release nifedipine (30 mg/day), and omeprazole (20 mg/day), and was discharged on long-term home oxygen therapy, but succumbed to progressive respiratory failure 8 weeks after discharge.
